summary: Provides a basic set of Media Gateway Control Protocol (MGCP) packages. Several are updates of packages from RFC 2705, including generic, line, trunk, handset, RTP, DTMF and announcement server packages, and five new ones are added. It is informational.

eli5.summary: MGCP lets a controller tell phone gateways what to do. Packages are toolkits of features like ringing and tones. This document hands out a basic set of ready-made toolkits.

subtitle: A toolkit of features for controlling media gateways that connect telephone networks.

tldr.problem: Media Gateway Control Protocol (MGCP) allows a central call controller to manage telephone gateways, but gateways need to support a wide range of features such as tones, DTMF digits, continuity testing, and announcements.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines 13 packages, each providing a set of signals (commands to the gateway) and events (notifications from the gateway). Packages cover generic media, DTMF, trunk signaling, line signaling, RTP, and announcements.
tldr.outcome: Gateway implementations can declare which packages they support, allowing call controllers to confidently use feature sets without needing to know vendor-specific extensions.

today: RFC 3660 defines the standard MGCP packages for basic media gateway control. While MGCP has been superseded by Megaco/H.248 (RFC 3525) as the preferred IETF standard, MGCP and these packages continue to be deployed in many telecom networks and devices. The RFC remains the reference for MGCP package definitions and interoperability requirements.

sections.title: Introduction to MGCP Packages
sections.content:
Media Gateway Control Protocol (MGCP) allows a central call agent to command and monitor media gateways, which are network devices that connect telephone networks to IP networks or other networks. For example, a gateway converts voice between traditional telephone lines and VoIP (Voice over IP).

MGCP uses a command-response model. The call agent sends commands to the gateway (such as "create a connection", "apply this tone", "detect DTMF digits"), and the gateway sends notifications back (such as "I detected the DTMF digit 5", "the connection ended").

This document updates and extends the packages from RFC 2705, which defined features grouped into reusable packages. Each package is a named set of signals (commands to apply a feature) and events (notifications of detected activity). For example, the DTMF package defines how to request generation of DTMF tones (used by callers to enter numbers) and detection of received DTMF tones.

By grouping features into packages, a gateway can declare which packages it supports, enabling interoperability. The RFC also identifies two packages from RFC 2705 that are not included here (MF and NAS), and adds five new packages beyond the original set.
sections.eli5: MGCP is a way for a phone switch to talk to phone gateways and tell them what to do. This RFC provides a menu of things gateways can do, organized into groups called packages so everyone builds them the same way.

sections.title: Signals and Events
sections.content:
Each package describes two types of features: signals and events. A signal is a command from the call agent to the gateway requesting it to apply an action or generate output (such as playing a tone or starting a timer). An event is an unsolicited notification from the gateway to the call agent indicating that an activity occurred (such as detecting a DTMF digit or a long connection duration).

Signals are categorized by type. An On-Off (OO) signal stays active until told to stop, parameterized with "+" (turn on) or "-" (turn off). A Time-Out (TO) signal automatically terminates after a specified duration (or an infinite default duration if not specified). A Brief (BR) signal is momentary. For example, a confirmation tone signal is brief; a congestion tone signal is time-out based and continues until canceled.

Package authors must ensure consistency between signal and event definitions. This document corrected some inconsistencies from RFC 2705 where certain signals were misclassified (such as changing intercept tone and preemption tone from On-Off to Time-Out). The document also ensured that all packages containing Time-Out signals include operation complete and operation failure events.
sections.eli5: Signals are orders the controller sends ("play a tone", "start a timer"). Events are things the gateway reports back ("I heard a DTMF 5", "the tone stopped"). Different signal types auto-stop or stay on until told to stop.

sections.title: Core Packages Overview
sections.content:
The Generic Media Package (G) defines signals and events for general-purpose media gateways: confirmation tone, congestion tone, fax detection, intercept tone, long-duration connection tracking, modem tone detection, operation complete and failure events, pattern detection, preemption tone, and ringback tone (either endpoint-directed or connection-directed).

The DTMF Package (D) handles Dual-Tone Multi-Frequency signals: detection and generation of DTMF digits (0-9, #, *, A-D). It includes events for detecting DTMF tone duration (useful for detecting long-pressed keys), an interdigit timer (Timer T), and a DTMF wildcard that matches any digit 0-9. The package specifies minimum tone durations (50 ms) and minimum inter-digit silence (45 ms) per telecom standards.

The Trunk Package (T) provides signals for telephone trunk lines: answer supervision, blocking (for one-way trunks), busy tone, continuity tones (2010 Hz for go-tone, 1780 Hz for return tone), loopback, milliwatt test tones, reorder tone, special information tone (used to signal call failures), quiet termination, and test patterns. These are used by telephone switches to manage trunk circuits.

The Line Package (L) provides signals for analog phone line interfaces: on-hook and off-hook detection, dial tone, busy tone, call waiting tones, handset effects (hookflash, handset on-hook/off-hook), and line equipment features.
sections.eli5: The RFC provides packages for different gateway types. Generic handles basic tones. DTMF handles phone button presses and detection. Trunk handles telephone trunk circuits. Line handles regular phone lines.

sections.title: Specialized Packages
sections.content:
The Handset Emulation Package (H) allows a gateway to emulate a telephone handset, detecting handset activities like on-hook, off-hook, hookflash (briefly hanging up while staying connected, used for features like call waiting), and handset speaker or microphone control.

The RTP Package (R) addresses Real-Time Transport Protocol concerns: per-packet loss and delay reporting, local and remote SSRC (Synchronization Source) identifiers, and RTP header information. This allows the gateway to report media quality metrics back to the controller.

The Announcement Server Package (A) enables a gateway endpoint to act as an automated announcement server (leaving messages, playing prompts), supporting announcements identified by names or numbers and allowing prerecorded messages to play.

The Script Package allows a gateway to execute simple scripts, enabling sequences of tones and detections to be orchestrated by the gateway rather than controlled step-by-step by the call agent.

New packages added in this document include the Signal List Package (SL) for requesting multiple signals in sequence, the Media Format Parameter Package (FM) for specifying codec and media format options (a LocalConnectionOption), the Resource Reservation Package (RES) for QoS resource reservation requests, and the Supplementary Services Tone Package (SST) for service tones like call waiting notification or call hold tones.
sections.eli5: More specialized packages handle handsets, RTP quality metrics, prerecorded announcements, script execution, and new capabilities like resource reservation and media format negotiation.

sections.title: Package Versioning and Interoperability
sections.content:
Several packages have been updated from RFC 2705, changing from version 0 (unversioned) to version 1 to reflect the changes and corrections. The generic, line, trunk, handset, RTP, DTMF, announcement server and script packages all received version updates. The new packages (signal list, resource reservation, media format, supplementary services, digit map extension) are defined only in this document.

The document improves interoperability by clarifying signal types and adding event definitions where missing. For example, some events in RFC 2705 packages required specific provisioning between the call agent and gateway; those provisioning requirements are now documented. In cases where events have aliases across packages, the document recommends which alias the call agent should use for new implementations, though gateways MUST implement all events in a package.

Package versions enable the call agent to audit which versions a gateway implements (if the gateway supports the auditing capability), ensuring the controller knows exactly which feature set behavior to expect from each gateway. This is particularly important for complex packages like DTMF (with timer thresholds and digit map interaction) and Trunk (with continuity testing procedures) where behavior depends on precise definitions.
sections.eli5: Packages now have version numbers so the controller can ask a gateway which version of each package it supports. This prevents confusion when the same package name means different things in different gateways or software versions.
